Los tres temas anteriores dieron el idio: The three previous topics gave you the language: propositions, sets and [[lg-demostracion|proofs]]. This one gives the method for when a problem comes without a label, and it serves for the whole course: heuristics do not depend on any particular technique.
Casi todo lo que se estudia en matemátic: Almost everything you study in mathematics is techniques for solving problems that already have a name: quadratic equations, systems, derivatives. But in an exam, and outside it, problems do not arrive with the label on. They arrive as a paragraph that looks like none of the ones you have done, and the feeling is of standing in front of a blank wall.
La buena noticia es que para esa pared t: The good news is that there is a method for that wall too. It is not an algorithm that guarantees the solution, but a collection of questions and strategies —the heuristics— that mathematicians use without saying so. This topic says them. And since they do not depend on any particular technique, they serve for the whole course: it is worth coming back here whenever a problem gets stuck.
<strong>Comprender el problema.</strong>: Understand the problem. What is the data? What exactly is being asked? What conditions are there? Draw a picture, name the things, tell it in your own words. A huge share of the stuck moments come from not having understood what is being asked.
<strong>Concebir un plan.</strong> ¿Has: Devise a plan. Have you seen a similar problem? Do you know one with the same unknown? If nothing comes to mind, try a heuristic from the list below.
<strong>Ejecutar el plan.</strong> Con c: Carry out the plan. Carefully, checking each step. If the plan does not work, you go back to the previous phase: that is not failing, it is the normal way of working.
<strong>Examinar la solución.</strong> ¿: Look back. Does the result make sense? Do the units add up? What happens in an extreme case? Could it have been done another way? This is the phase most often skipped and the one that catches most errors.
Una respuesta que dice que un coche reco: An answer saying that a car covers 3000 km in an hour, that a probability is 1.4, or that a tank holds −5 litres is wrong, even if the arithmetic looks correct. Stopping for ten seconds to look at the result with common sense is the cheapest check there is. [[ar-magnitudes|Dimensional analysis]] is its version with units.
Las cuatro fases, aplicadas a un problem: The four phases, applied to a problem
Un depósito se llena en 3 horas con un g: A tank fills in 3 hours with one tap and in 6 hours with another. How long does it take to fill with both open at once?
<strong>Comprender.</strong> Datos: un g: Understand. Data: one tap takes 3 h, the other 6 h. Asked for: the time with both. A first intuition: it has to be less than 3 h, because the second tap helps. The temptation to add (9 h) or to average (4.5 h) already fails to fit that.
Antes de calcular nada: ¿el resultado se: Before calculating anything: will the result be more or less than 3 hours?
<strong>Plan.</strong> Los tiempos no se: Plan. Times do not add, but what each tap fills per hour does. In one hour the first fills $\frac{1}{3}$ of the tank and the second $\frac{1}{6}$. We name the unknown: with both, $\frac{1}{t}$ is filled per hour.
¿Qué cantidad sí se puede sumar entre lo: Which quantity can be added between the two taps?
<strong>Examinar.</strong> Dos horas es: Look back. Two hours is less than 3, as predicted, and more than half of 3 (if the two taps were the same they would take 1.5 h; the second is slower, so a bit more). It fits. Direct check: in 2 h the first fills $\frac{2}{3}$ and the second $\frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$; total, 1 tank. ✓
¿Cómo comprobarías el resultado sin repe: How would you check the result without repeating the same calculation?
La cuarta fase no es un adorno: es la qu: The fourth phase is not decoration: it is what would have caught the 9 or the 4.5 if we had rushed.
Estas cuatro fases las escribió George P: These four phases were written by George Pólya, a Hungarian mathematician teaching at Stanford, in a 1945 book titled How to Solve It. Pólya had noticed that his students knew many techniques but did not know when to use them, and that good mathematicians always ask themselves the same questions without realising it. He decided to write them down. The book has sold over a million copies and is still the starting point of any course on problem solving.
Heurísticas: qué probar cuando no se te: Heuristics: what to try when nothing comes to mind
Si el problema habla de $n$ objetos, pru: If the problem talks about $n$ objects, try with 1, with 2, with 3. You see the mechanism, sometimes a pattern appears and, above all, you understand what it is about. How many handshakes are there at a meeting of 20 people if everybody greets everybody? With 2 people there is 1; with 3, 3; with 4, 6. Each person greets the other $n - 1$, and so each handshake gets counted twice: $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$, which for 20 gives 190.
Pero un patrón es una sospecha, no una p: But a pattern is a suspicion, not a proof. The example below shows this in the most forceful way, and that is why [[lg-demostracion|proof methods]] exist: to turn the suspicion into certainty.
Un patrón que miente: las regiones del c: A pattern that lies: the regions of the circle

Con 1, 2, 3, 4 y 5 puntos salen 1, 2, 4,: With 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 points you get 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 regions. Write down how many you think there will be with 6 points before moving the slider.

Si se conoce el final y se pide el princ: If the end is known and the beginning is asked for, you walk the problem backwards undoing each step. “I spent half my money and 3 € more, and I have 5 € left.” Backwards: before spending the 3 € I had 8; since that was half, at the start I had 16. It is also the strategy of proofs: you look at what would be needed to reach the conclusion, and what would be needed for that.
Un <strong>invariante</strong> es algo q: An invariant is something that does not change however many operations you perform: a parity, a sum, a colour. If at the start it is one thing and in the desired situation it is another, that situation is impossible, with no need to try every route. It is the most elegant heuristic, and the one that proves something cannot be done.
Quita las dos esquinas opuestas, que son: Remove the two opposite corners, which are the same colour. Can the rest be covered with dominoes? And if you remove two neighbouring squares?
Se quitan dos casillas de un tablero de: Two squares are removed from an 8×8 board. Can the rest be covered with dominoes, each two squares long? Choose which squares to remove and count the colours: each domino always covers one white and one black.
una blanca y una negra lejanas: one white and one black, far apart

Si hay más palomas que agujeros, algún a: If there are more pigeons than holes, some hole has at least two pigeons. It sounds silly and it is a serious tool: in any group of 13 people, two have their birthday in the same month; in Madrid there are at least two people with exactly the same number of hairs on their head, because there are more inhabitants than hairs a head can hold.
Ponerle nombre a lo que no sabes: Give a name to what you do not know
Llamar $x$ a la incógnita y escribir las: Calling the unknown $x$ and writing the conditions as if it were already known is the heuristic that gave rise to [[al-lenguaje|algebra]]. And it has variants: drawing the figure already finished, assuming the problem solved and seeing what properties the solution would have.
Modelizar: del mundo a las matemáticas y: Modelling: from the world to mathematics and back
Un problema de la vida real no viene esc: A real-life problem does not come written in formulas. Modelling is translating it, and it is a cycle, not a straight line:
<strong>Simplificar</strong> la situació: Simplify the situation: decide what matters and what can be neglected, and make the assumptions explicit.
<strong>Matematizar</strong>: poner nomb: Mathematise: name the variables and write the relations between them.
<strong>Resolver</strong> el problema ma: Solve the mathematical problem, with the techniques of the course.
<strong>Interpretar</strong> el resultad: Interpret the result in context: what that number means.
<strong>Validar</strong>: ¿se parece a l: Validate: does it look like reality? If not, the assumptions are revised and you start again.
Enrico Fermi, premio Nobel de Física, pr: Enrico Fermi, Nobel laureate in physics, used to ask his students things like “how many piano tuners are there in Chicago?”. There was no data: you had to estimate how many inhabitants, how many pianos per household, how often one is tuned and how many a professional can tune in a year, and multiply. The errors in each assumption tend to cancel out and the result usually gets the order of magnitude right. That kind of quick estimate is a much-sought skill in engineering, in consultancy and in science: before a long calculation, knowing what result would be reasonable.
Estas cuatro fases valen para cualquier: These four phases work for any problem. When the problem is an exam, there is also a list of concrete mistakes that repeat year after year and cost more marks than not knowing: they are collected and classified in [[pau-errores|the errors that cost most marks]], with the distinction that is almost never explained —getting a calculation wrong costs little; getting an idea wrong can void the whole part—.
Cuando el problema es un examen: When the problem is an exam
Releer, dibujar y decir con tus palabras: Re-reading, drawing and saying in your own words what is being asked costs a minute and stops you solving a different problem from the one in front of you.
Las regiones del círculo dan 1, 2, 4, 8,: The regions of the circle give 1, 2, 4, 8, 16… and then 31. Five cases that fit prove nothing; they only suggest what to prove.
3,5 personas, una longitud negativa o un: 3.5 people, a negative length or a probability of 1.4 warn you of an error sooner than any review of the arithmetic.
La mirada atrás es la fase que más enseñ: Looking back is the phase that teaches most: could it have been done another way? Does the method work for other problems? That is where a problem turns into a technique.
